It may be necessary to thoroughly reorganize the system of appointing and training marine corps officers.

The unfortunate case of Mr. Sutton can be cleared up by the present board of inquiry with perhaps few courts martial for the officers who have on the stand confessed to violations of the regulations, but the root of the evil—the system—can, to my mind, only be corrected by thorough investigation by congress.

Don't Like Brutality.
In discussing the question of brutality another senator said:

There is a disposition on the part of legislators here to frown upon any form of brutality in any branch of the government service. It may be all right for the Germans to encourage fighting among their cadets and officers, but we will not tolerate it in this country. The idea prevails that the Sutton incident is only unusual in that it resulted in death. I trust we will find time to go thoroughly into the matter.

It was largely through the influence and hard work of Senator Jonathan Bourne, Jr., of Oregon that the Sutton case was reopened by the navy department. The Suttons have lived in Portland for many years, their being prominent in railroad affairs on the coast.

After spending Saturday in Washington, Judge Advocate Henry Leonard and the attorneys of the Sutton family, Henry E. Davis and Van Dyke Brothers, returned tonight to Annapolis, where the inquiry will be resumed tomorrow morning.

Four More Witnesses.

The government has yet four witnesses uncalled. The two most important are Lieut. Uttley and Surgeon Cook, who are returning from a European cruise on the battleship New Hampshire. They cannot reach Annapolis before Aug. 1 and will probably be the last witnesses heard.

Uttley was one of the officers who rode out from the Carvel hall barroom in Sutton's automobile. He had hands, according to testimony, in the first fight near the College Greek bridge and was on the scene of the death fight, which occurred a few minutes later.

Surgeon Cook performed the autopsy the morning after the young marine died. His testimony is wanted particularly to determine the number of wounds on Sutton's body and their nature.

Another government witness is Ernest Fogg, a Washington club man, who saw much of Sutton when the latter was at the capitol waiting for his designation to the school of application at Annapolis. Young is said to be in poor health and may be unable to attend.

Mrs. Parker the star Witness.

Mrs. Rose Sutton Parker of St. Paul, sister of the dead lieutenant, promises to be the star witness for their side. She hurried to Annapolis after learning of the tragedy and soon heard rumors that caused her to doubt the suicide verdict of the first board of inquiry, which was begun few hours after Sutton's death and ended before the people of Annapolis and the outside world knew that the young marine was killed.

She talked to Maj. Doyen, in command of the marine barracks at Annapolis and in charge of the student officers. She sent for the officers who had been concerned in the fight. She declares that he discussed the death of her brother in a most brutal fashion and told her that differed materially from that which he told on the stand. BY A W. LAMOUREUX. Paris, Oct 16.—The efforts of the anti-militarists to obtain real hold over the young conscripts are matter of common knowledge, and though they are rarely attended with success, since nearly every Frenchman is at heart a soldier, they are from time to time made evident at Macon, when the regimental colors were found soiled and torn.

Le Temps regrets the days when, under the influence of Gambetta and the memory of 1870, the Army was regarded as being above all party policies. Now, however, the Army has become battlefield for the two extreme parties in France, and Le Temps compares an appeal to the conscripts published by the notorious anti-militarist paper "La Guerre Sociale" with manifestoes posted in Bordeaux, for which the extreme Clericals it says must be held responsible. The anti-militarist appeal, with astounding impotence, calls on the young conscripts to form revolutionary sections in their companies and regiments, "such as already exist in certain fortresses on the Eastern frontier. These sections, though autonomous, are in relation with one another, and form a force which, on the day when our Government dreams of war abroad or at home, will rise and declare that they are not alone and must be reckoned with."

The Bordeaux poster, on the other hand, calls on Roman Catholic fathers of families to appoint formally the garrison chaplain as correspondent for their sons, so that they may receive remittances from home through him.

Another manifesto addressed to the conscripts themselves bids them have all their correspondence addressed "care of the chaplain."

These posters are, Le Temps points out, direct incentive to breach of discipline, since by the military regulations soldiers are forbidden to receive anything through any other person than the quartermaster. It is clear, says Le Temps, that the object of both the anti-militarist and the Clerical manifestoes is to remove the men as far as possible from the influence of their superior officers. "It is the substitution for an education intended to produce unity, through a common sentiment of patriotic duty, of another education which can only tend to increase the divisions that trouble the country."

The French Budget.

The new Finance Minister M. Cochery intends to meet the deficit of 40,000,000 in the French Budget by means of various fresh taxes and increases in existing taxation, including an augmentation of death duties. Since the year 1901 these duties have been considerably augmented, and are progressive in the double sense that they increase with the amount inherited and with the remoteness of the relationship between the testator and the beneficiary. A wife inheriting from a husband inheriting from a wife pays duty which ranges from 3 3/4 per cent to 9 per cent according to the amount inherited, and the incidence of the duty increased until, in the case of relations beyond the sixth degree or of unrelated beneficiaries, the tax ranges from 15 per cent in the case of inheritances valued at $400 or under to 20 1/2 per cent in the case of estates valued at over $100,000. M. Cochery now proposes to raise the scale of all death duties leviable on estates above the value of $400.

The minimum augmentation will be in the duty on estates the value of which is between $20,000 and $100,000, and which are inherited in the direct line of succession; here the increase will be 1/2 per cent. the King's work. The kingdom of
heaven was near them, because the
King was about to appear. He was
about to set up His kingdom in the
hearts of those who would receive
Him. Furthermore, He would have
set up His kingdom on earth if He
had been accepted by His people.
More than seven centuries had passed
since Isaiah (Isa. 40:3-5) had uttered
his prophecy of coming of the Lord
and of the forerunner who should
precede Him. He had come at last.
God's word had been fulfilled to the
letter, as it always will be sooner or
later, though the fulfillment may wait
for centuries as in this case. John
came in the spirit and the appearance
of Elijah of old (Comp. 2 Kgs.;
Matt. 17:12, 13). His whole manner
of life was a protest against the pre-
vailing worldliness and self-indul-
gence. Jesus did not follow in the
footsteps of John in the outward man-
ner of His protest. But men who
would represent God and have power
with men should live lives of great
simplicity. John's earnestness, rug-
gedness, fearlessness, renunciation of
self and stern declaration in the pow-
er of the Spirit of the message God
gave him awakened great interest.
Men were convinced that he was "a
man sent from God."


III. Bring Forth Fruit Meet For
Repentance, 7-10. John was no trim-
mer. He was not an adept at honeyed
words (cf. Matt. 3:7; 3:8; Jno.
3:10). John believed in a coming
wrath of God against sin. It was not
any more popular doctrine in that
day than it is now, but it was true,
and men needed to hear about it, and
so this faithful man of God told them.
"The way to flee from the wrath to
come" and to "prepare the way of the
Lord" and to be ready for "the king-
dom" was to repent with that genuine
repentance that would show itself in
a transformed life, bringing forth
fruit worthy of repentance. No one
was ever saved by pious ancestry.
A son of Abraham may be a child of
the devil (Jno. 8:37, 38, 41, 44).


III. The Baptism With the Holy
Wind and Fire, 11, 12. John has
emphasized the need of good fruit;
he now discloses the secret of bearing
it, A mightier than he was coming
who would baptize with something
more efficacious than water—"with
the Holy Spirit and in fire." Some have
interpreted these words to mean that
there are two baptisms between which
one may have his choice—"the bap-
tism in the Spirit" (now) or "the bap-
tism in the fire of judgment" (hereafter). The orig-
inal does not admit of this interpre-
tation. John doubtless had in mind
Isaiah's expression, "the Spirit of
burning" (Isa. 4:4) when he uttered
these words. In verse 11 we have
three baptismal elements, "water"
with which John should baptize them
unto repentance; the "Holy Wind"
and "fire" with which Jesus would
baptize them. In Acts 2:2, 3, we
have the fulfillment of the promise in
the case of the apostles when they
found themselves engulfed in a
mighty "wind" from heaven, "tongues
of fire" resting upon their heads, and they themselves
"filled with the Holy Wind." The promise
is not to two different baptisms, one
of blessing and the other of cursing,
but of one two-fold baptism of bless-
ing, "Holy Ghost and fire." But what
does it mean to be baptized in fire?
The answer is found in considering
the work that "fire" does. (1) "Fire"
reveals (1 Cor. 3:13). (2)
"Fire" refines (Isa. 4:4; Zech. 13:9;
Mal. 3:1-3), (3) "Fire" consumes
filthiness and scum (Zech. 13:9-11).
(4) "Fire" illuminates. (5) "Fire"
makes to glow and melt (Jer. 23:29).
(6) "Fire" generates energy. A bap-
tism in "fire" then reveals us to our
selves; consumes the filthiness and
scum—the selfishness, ambition,
worldliness and vileness that we have
vainly contended against for years,
out of us; makes us to burn and glow
with love to God and man and truth,
love for souls; fills us with heavenly
energy.

The reception committee went aboard the vessel on her arrival yesterday morning and the twelve candidates, headed by Warrant Machinist F. I. Ingram, came ashore in full uniform at 6 o'clock p. m. For an hour last night one of the worst storms in years ragged over Great Salt Lake. Lashed and whipped under driving gale, America's Dead Sea piled its waves in a fury that brought terror to over 1000 pleasure seekers at the Saltair beach resort, and imperiled the lives of thousand bathers. During that hour of fearsome dread the launch Irene, with passengers on board, buffeted its way against the waves and rolling seas and only by the skill of its master succeeded in a safe landing. The fury and strength of the storm is told in the carrying away of 900 feet of staunch platform. That no fatality resulted is due to the prompt, energetic and in several instances heroic work of the officials and attaches of the beach resort.

The storm, almost unprecedented, broke with startling suddenness; it was the veritable thunderbolt from the clear sky. The day was one of sultry heat with cloudless sky until towards sunset the dark clouds with the faint flash of the lightning and the distant thunder. It was all so distant and far away that the pleasure seekers paid little heed and the bathers continued their sport in the water.

MID WAVES AND DARKNESS.
In an instant, however, the storm loosened, and in the same instant the wind swept across the lake, piling the water into waves that literally hurled the bathers before them. The terror was added to by the sudden darkness, and it was in the agony of fright that the bathers battled to reach the bathhouses. The majority of those in the water succeeded in reaching the bathhouses, but several found themselves unable to fight the strength of the waves. Some of these were carried by the waves to the shore; others, but for the heroic efforts of Earnest Larson, in charge of a little gasoline launch used for the purpose of caring for the bathers, would have succumbed to the water.

BATHERS SEEK PAVILION.
Those who reached the bathhouses safely still found themselves in a precarious condition as the waves were over the flooring of the houses and seemed to threaten the carrying away of the structure. Gathering what clothing they could, many of those who had been in the water sought safety in the main pavilion clad only in their bathing suits.

During the storm the visitors at Saltair huddled themselves in the main pavilion, and looked upon the storm with terror. When it was recalled that the launch Irene was out on the lake with passengers on board, the alarm increased until the staunch little boat was seen coming out of the darkness breasting the waves safely under the guidance of Captain Anderson. As the craft was moored and her passengers began to land on the pier, cheer after cheer went out into the air.

STORY OF PASSENGERS.
It was a thrilling story the passengers had to tell. The Irene was about 10 miles out when the storm began. Many women were among the passengers, and in the first few minutes the crowd became panic-stricken. Capt. Anderson quickly ordered everyone below the deck, and then himself took the wheel. Confined as they were, and with the little craft tossed like cork, a number of the women became seasick, and one or two fainted. Through the skilful handling of his boat, however, Capt. Anderson rode out the storm and brought his passengers in safely.

STEAMER VISTA BEACHED.
About the only damage resulting from the storm was the bleaching of the steamer Vista, and the carrying away of the platform leading from the pavilion to the bunk houses used by the employees. When the latter was destroyed one of the employees was on the platform and was thrown into the water. He managed to reach the shore in safety and escaped without injury.
